clue.text: Try to attend

definitions.meaning: a judge tries a case in court
to attend is to listen or pay heed

explanation.definitionFit: A court that tries a case listens to it formally, and paying attention to a speaker is listening too.

clue.text: Small volume is a part of ten's armoury

definitions.text: Small volume is a part of ten's armoury

parts.words: Small volume is a part of ten's armoury
parts.note: reads as a little book on the shelf, but 'ten' is short for tennis and the small volume is a stroke: a reduced form of a shot hit before the ball bounces

explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' tempts towards books or sound; here it is played on to mean a partial version of a volley, a stroke in a tennis player's repertoire ('ten's armoury').
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis stroke struck just as the ball rises off the court belongs among a player's shots.

clue.text: Plug it up against the outside

indicators.note: the word for against forms the outside, with the other piece placed within it

parts.note: adverse means opposed or against

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the little word it is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for blocking a hole by pushing a bung upward against the outer face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the little word over in this down clue, and 'the outside' wraps the word for against round it. 'Plug' looks like a bung, but it is the verb meaning to promote.
explanation.definitionFit: To plug a product is to promote it loudly, which is to publicise it.

clue.text: I mess about, though in a way that's restrained

indicators.note: in a different way or manner, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: Someone who fools around yet manages to stay controlled while doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges I MESS ABOUT; 'about' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstemious person is moderate, holding back from food and drink.

clue.text: Gets suits

definitions.meaning: to get as in 'gets angry', meaning turns into
a colour suits you when it looks good on you

explanation.definitionFit: One verb means both 'turns into' (she gets tired) and 'flatters' (that hat flatters you).

clue.text: Tell sir about latticework in the garden

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to inform a gentleman regarding the wooden framework among his plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A trellis is a lattice frame on which garden climbers are trained.

clue.text: It's an imitation, of course

parts.note: 'of course' seems to mean naturally, but it means a dish served as a course of a meal, one made in imitation of a turtle-based broth

explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally' but means a course of a dinner: a soup made from calf's head to imitate the real turtle version.
explanation.definitionFit: The dish is a Victorian imitation broth served as a starter at dinner.

clue.text: Had day off — like a duck?

indicators.note: off says the letter for day is removed from the other word

parts.note: a duckling is covered in down, so downed means feathered with down

explanation.surface: Someone took a day off work and spent it like a duck, perhaps paddling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like a duck' gives DOWNED (covered in down); 'off' takes away its D for day.
explanation.definitionFit: Had in the past tense of possessing: something you had, you owned.

clue.text: A place to buy grass

definitions.meaning: British slang: to inform on someone to the police

explanation.definitionFit: A store is somewhere to make purchases, and in British slang to betray a criminal to police is also this verb.

clue.text: Experts wanting cue in play walk to part of a stage

parts.note: pros are professionals, experts

indicators.note: in play suggests letters moving loosely and so rearranged

parts.note: to march is to walk in step

explanation.surface: Professionals in a theatre lack their prompt and walk on to the boards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' rearranges the five letters of 'cue in'; 'wanting' only joins. The proscenium arch frames the front of a traditional theatre stage.
explanation.definitionFit: This arch frames the front of a theatre stage, separating it from the auditorium.

clue.text: Tennis player starting to lose and swear

indicators.note: the start of the next word gives its opening letter

parts.note: to aver is to declare solemnly, to swear

explanation.surface: A tennis player begins to lose a match and curses.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod Laver is an Australian tennis great who won the Grand Slam twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Rod Laver is one of the most famous tennis champions.

clue.text: Notes the volume going up?

parts.note: looks like a comment on rising prices or a book, but describes a musical passage marked to become gradually louder

explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like a verb (observes); it is musical notes, and 'volume' is loudness, not a book.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the marking means a gradual increase in loudness.

clue.text: I must deliver one broadcast about centre of Halifax with semblance of truth

indicators.note: about means going around, so the anagram encloses the next piece
broadcast as in seed scattered widely, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: the central letter of the town's name

explanation.surface: A radio presenter must announce a piece about Halifax, a town in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' rearranges I MUST DELIVER plus I (one); 'about' puts that around I, the 'centre of' Halifax.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the quality of seeming real, an appearance of reality.

clue.text: Clear soldiers, with time, from the village

parts.note: to settle a bill is to clear it
men is the usual crossword word for soldiers

explanation.surface: An order to drive troops out of a village after a while.
explanation.definitionFit: A small community of people living together is a settlement, such as a village.

clue.text: Hangs around cloisters, but not Catholic school

indicators.note: but not means the letters for these two words are left out

explanation.surface: Someone lingers in the cloisters of a church but avoids the Catholic school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' removes C and the first S from CLOISTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To loiter is to linger aimlessly, idling in a place.

clue.text: Come up for air — like the champion of Bondi?

definitions.meaning: a diver rises to the top of the water
Bondi is a famous Sydney beach

explanation.definitionFit: A swimmer rises to the top of the water to breathe; split in two, the word is a top wave rider.

clue.text: I'm in a country making cartoons

indicators.note: in places the first piece within the second

parts.note: a nation is a country
taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone abroad says they are drawing comic strips there.
explanation.definitionFit: Animation is the art of making moving cartoons, a collective term for them.

clue.text: Ironing in the twilight

definitions.meaning: ironing out creases, making smooth or level
the time of day as light fades

explanation.definitionFit: Smoothing out creases makes things level, and dusk is the part of the day after sunset.

clue.text: Collects gun belonging to girl

parts.note: gat is old American slang for a gun
something belonging to her is hers

explanation.surface: Someone takes possession of a firearm owned by a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To collect things is to bring them together, to assemble them.

clue.text: Some Purcell is tricky for Lloyd Webber?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Henry Purcell's music is said to be difficult for Andrew Lloyd Webber.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the composer Andrew Lloyd Webber; the definition points to his brother Julian, a famous classical musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Julian Lloyd Webber is a renowned performer on the cello, so the word describes him.

clue.text: Lace she obtained from upmarket part of London

indicators.note: obtained from says the answer is got by reworking these letters

explanation.surface: A woman bought her lace in a smart district of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea is a wealthy district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelsea is an affluent area of west London.

clue.text: Part of bill's passage?

parts.note: suggests a section of a bird's beak or a payment, but a parliamentary bill passes through phases on its way to law

explanation.walkthrough: In the UK Parliament a bill is examined clause by clause by a small group of members after its second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the phase where a group of legislators scrutinises a bill in detail.

clue.text: Outrageous queen's fur

parts.note: OTT stands for over the top, meaning outrageous
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen

explanation.surface: A monarch's coat of animal pelt is shocking.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelt of this river mammal is used as a fur.

clue.text: Damage limb at hospital

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital
an arm is a limb

explanation.surface: An arm injured and treated at a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: To damage something is to hurt or injure it.

clue.text: Lawyers are snotty when drunk

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters are reeling about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Lawyers become rude and arrogant after drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Attorneys are legal representatives, chiefly an American term for solicitors.

clue.text: Join united nations? That's about time!

parts.note: UN is the short form for the world body of states; the letters at the start of the first word matching the answer is a coincidence, not a hidden word

indicators.note: about means going round, so the letters for that's surround the next piece

parts.note: i.e., Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: An impatient cry that the world's nations should finally come together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the abbreviation for 'that is' (Latin id est) round the T; the exclamation 'That's about time!' disguises it.
explanation.definitionFit: To join is to bring together, to combine into one.

clue.text: Potato and cabbage salad? If it can go wrong, it will!

definitions.text: If it can go wrong, it will!

parts.note: murphy is slang for a potato, from the Irish association
slaw, short for coleslaw, is a cabbage salad

explanation.surface: A side order of spuds and coleslaw, with a gloomy forecast of disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The adage that anything that can go wrong will is named after an engineer called Murphy.

clue.text: Return to smack insect

indicators.note: return means the word for smack is read backwards

parts.note: a smack is a taste or flavour, a tang

explanation.surface: Getting back to swatting a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smack' looks like a slap, but here it is a flavour; 'Return' reverses TANG.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnat is a small biting fly.
